title: Choosing a Structure: A Decision Procedure

questions.question: A BIN table is implemented as a HashMap keyed by the first six digits of the card number. Which change in the data breaks it?
options: Card numbers that start with a zero, which the map cannot store as a key
Issuer ranges that share a six-digit prefix but differ at the seventh or eighth digit
A monthly reload that doubles the number of entries in the file
Card numbers longer than sixteen digits, which overflow the key
questions.explanation: A map keyed by a fixed six-digit prefix can hold one value per prefix, so two eight-digit ranges under the same six digits collide and one is lost; this is the 8-digit BIN migration incident. Hash maps handle growth and any string key, and the key length does not depend on the PAN length.

questions.question: What is the first step of the decision procedure, before any structure is named?
options: Estimate memory per entry so the structure fits the heap
Pick the structure with the best Big-O for lookup
List every operation with its frequency, latency budget, and working set
Check whether the standard library already provides an implementation
questions.explanation: The access pattern is the input to every later step; invariants and constants are evaluated against it. Memory and library availability are Step 3 (constants), and Big-O for a single operation is how the BIN table ended up as a hash map.

questions.question: A retry scheduler uses a binary heap keyed by due time. Cancelling a job by id is O(n). Which fix keeps the heap and makes cancel cheap?
options: Replace the heap with a hash map keyed by job id, since cancel is now the dominant operation
Add a hash set of cancelled ids and skip those jobs when they reach the top (lazy deletion)
Rebuild the heap from scratch after each cancel so the removed job is gone
Sort the heap array after each cancel so the job can be found by binary search
questions.explanation: Lazy deletion makes cancel O(1) and costs only the memory of ids that have not yet surfaced; a hash map from id to heap index is the other standard fix. Replacing the heap loses extract-min, and rebuilding or sorting after each cancel is O(n) or worse.

questions.question: Why is a tree keyed by timestamp the wrong primary structure for an append-only audit log?
options: Trees cannot store more than a few million entries before running out of heap
Timestamps are not unique, and a tree cannot store duplicate keys under any scheme
Range queries by time are impossible on a tree and require a hash map
Append order already is time order, so the tree spends its work maintaining an order the log has for free
questions.explanation: A log answers time-range queries with a binary search for the start and a sequential scan, with no per-append cost; an unbalanced tree degenerates on monotonic inserts and a balanced one rotates for nothing. Duplicate timestamps are handled by a composite key, and trees do support range queries.

questions.question: An idempotency store must hold 50 million keys for 24 hours and survive a process restart. What does the constants step conclude?
options: Use an in-process HashMap with a background thread that sweeps expired keys every minute, since 50 million entries fit on a large heap
Use a TreeMap keyed by expiry time so the oldest entries can be removed first and lookups by key stay logarithmic
The working set and the durability invariant put the hash map in an external store with TTL (Redis SET NX EX, or a unique-indexed table)
Use a sorted array of keys, since 50 million entries fit in memory and binary search is fast enough for the 1 ms budget
questions.explanation: At roughly 250 bytes per entry the set is about 12 GB, and surviving a restart is an invariant no in-process structure meets; the access pattern is still exact-key putIfAbsent, so the structure is a hash map, externalised. A tree keyed by expiry degenerates on monotonic time, and a sorted array has O(n) inserts.

questions.question: What belongs in the design note's "impossible operation" section, and why?
options: The operations the structure makes O(n) or cannot express, so a later request for one triggers a redesign instead of a workaround
Every operation the structure supports, with its complexity, so reviewers can confirm the API is complete and matches the table
The Big-O of each operation copied from the textbook table for the structure, so the note is self-contained for new readers
A list of competing structures that were considered, with their benchmark results, so the choice can be defended in review
questions.explanation: Naming what the structure cannot do cheaply is what makes a future change recognisable as a change of access pattern. Supported operations and complexities are the access-pattern table; rejected candidates have their own section.
